chapter: The war years: Barnet, Hot Lips Page, Newton and Kirby
title: Frankie Newton's politics and bitterness
summary: Newton was involved with left politics, grew bitter from Southern racism, and was cruel to some like George Wein.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: How would Frank have got that job at that time? Had he got a bit of a name?
Frankie?
Yeah.
He had a good name with the workers -- fellow workers!
Yeah. I know when I came back after the war he was involved in this stuff. I couldn't understand it.
Yeah. Camp Unity and all that, addressing workers. He was a Walenska(?), right?
Ramirez - 105
Didn't that do him harm?
He didn't get too far.
Well, I know when I came back, I met him... Now, he wanted me to go downtown and play ping-pong! I couldn't understand. I thought "Now, something has happened to this guy. This is a shame!"
Yeah, he was...
And they were painting down there or something; they were expressing themselves by painting. So I don't know. I never did go down with him.
Frank was always strange, he had this strange ideas, but we didn't mind it.
Yeah. But what on earth... In '37, he wasn't... He was a fairly normal cat then.
Yeah, but he got very bitter later on.
Oh, did he.
Yeah, Frank got bitter. He used to cry.
Well, what made him bitter?
Well, he came up from the South, and I mean, the racism down there was... It used to drive him to tears.
And then he got beaten up by some soldiers or something.
No...
Did you hear about that?
Ramirez - 106
No.
Oh yeah. I heard that during the War he got beaten up. You know, he was a big fellow, and I guess they probably picked on him or something.

I don't know what trouble he got in. But he was very bitter. Very bitter. And he would take it out on somebody that he didn't like, you know. And I used to squirm at the things he used to say, you know. But with me he was great. I used to feel embarrassed for him. Do you feel like that with people?
Yes. You mean when...

Yeah. You squirm in your seat, you know. Until today, this is what I think... The things that he used to say to George Wein, you know, when Wein was in uniform; you know, I didn't particularly... He was so bitter. I don't know... You know, the poor boy squirmed, you know...!
